title: Derive the MOSFET I–V law and identify where it breaks
summary: Develop the gradual-channel model from inversion charge, obtain triode/saturation and transconductance, then test short-channel and body-bias limits.
objectives: Derive I–V by integrating inversion charge rather than memorizing it.
Compute saturation boundaries and bias headroom.
Extract gm, gm/ID and a first-order output resistance.
Explain body effect, DIBL and velocity saturation as distinct phenomena.

sections.title: 1. Prerequisites: the MOS electrostatic boundary
sections.html:
An ideal enhancement NMOS is formed in p-type silicon under a gate dielectric. A positive gate-to-source bias changes the electrostatic surface potential; beyond a threshold approximation it supports an electron inversion channel. The threshold is not a universal material constant: it responds to substrate doping, oxide thickness, gate work function, trapped charge, body bias, temperature, channel geometry and drain-induced barrier lowering.

In an ideal strong-inversion charge-sheet model, with source at \(V_S=0\) and local channel potential \(V(x)\), the magnitude of mobile inversion charge per area is approximately \(|Q_i(x)|=C'_{ox}[V_{GS}-V_T-V(x)]\). We assume constant mobility, negligible depletion-charge variation along the channel, a long device, a gradual electric field and charge near the Si–oxide interface. The bracket must remain nonnegative wherever the charge-sheet approximation is used.

sections.title: 2. Relate channel charge to current
sections.html:
A slice of inversion channel has mobile charge per unit length \(W|Q_i(x)|\). Under the local drift approximation, its current is \(I_D=\mu_n W|Q_i(x)|\,\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}x\). This is a conventional drain-current magnitude with \(V\) increasing from source to drain.

Substitute the charge relation, define overdrive \(V_{OV}=V_{GS}-V_T\), multiply by \(\mathrm{d}x\), and integrate from source to drain: \(I_D\int_0^L\mathrm{d}x=\mu_n WC'_{ox}\int_0^{V_{DS}}(V_{OV}-V)\,\mathrm{d}V\). Evaluating the integral gives \(I_D=(\mu_n C'_{ox}W/L)[V_{OV}V_{DS}-V_{DS}^2/2]\), the ideal triode/linear-region law.

Check units: \(\mu_n C'_{ox}(W/L)\) has units A/V². Multiplying by volts squared gives amperes. Do this check before typing a number; confusing \(C'_{ox}\) per unit area with device-total capacitance breaks the derivation.

sections.title: 3. Why the long-channel current saturates
sections.html:
At the drain end \(x=L\), charge-sheet inversion approaches zero when \(V_{DS}=V_{OV}\). Substituting the boundary into the triode expression yields \(I_{D,sat}=\tfrac12\mu_n C'_{ox}(W/L)V_{OV}^2\). Beyond this ideal boundary, the extra drain bias drops mainly across a near-drain high-field region; the simplest long-channel model treats the terminal current as constant.

**Saturation here does not mean unlimited voltage tolerance or absolute current independence.** Channel-length modulation increases drain current with \(V_{DS}\), and velocity saturation changes scaling for short channels. The square-law derivation only controls a limited operating regime. Its actual use is to understand bias trends, not to predict modern nanometer-CMOS signoff accuracy.

sections.title: 4. Differential parameters: gm, gds and intrinsic gain
sections.html:
For the ideal saturation expression, \(g_m=(\partial I_D/\partial V_{GS})_{V_{DS}}=\mu_n C'_{ox}(W/L)V_{OV}=2I_D/V_{OV}\). Thus \(g_m/I_D=2/V_{OV}\) in strong-inversion square-law conditions. It is a useful first-order efficiency measure: high transconductance for a given bias current can help analog gain, but bandwidth, noise, inversion level and matching impose competing constraints.

A first-order channel-length modulation model uses \(I_D\approx I_{D0}(1+\lambda V_{DS})\). Locally \(g_{ds}\approx\lambda I_{D0}\), so \(r_o\approx1/(\lambda I_D)\) when \(\lambda V_{DS}\) is small and the approximation is consistently applied. Intrinsic small-signal voltage gain magnitude is roughly \(g_mr_o\); it declines as finite output conductance grows.

sections.title: 5. Body bias and the depletion region
sections.html:
For an NMOS in a p-type body, increasing reverse source-to-body voltage \(V_{SB}>0\) generally expands depletion charge and increases threshold. The classical expression is \(V_T(V_{SB})=V_{T0}+\gamma[\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_{SB}}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}]\). Here \(2\phi_F\) is a positive magnitude in that convention. The body-effect coefficient \(\gamma\) depends on semiconductor and oxide parameters.

A source-follower whose source rises can therefore experience both reduced \(V_{GS}\) and increased \(V_T\). These are separate effects. Some modern devices have heavily engineered bodies or alternative structures; apply the model only when its premises are valid.

sections.title: 6. Scaling breaks assumptions in several different ways
sections.html:
Shorter channels experience strong lateral fields. Carrier speed ceases to increase linearly with field (velocity saturation), drain electric field lowers the source-channel barrier (DIBL), and junction electrostatics encroach into the channel (short-channel rolloff). Gate leakage, subthreshold current, quantum effects and parasitic resistances can also matter. A model that fits one I–V curve does not uniquely identify which mechanism is responsible.

An effective simulator comparison varies one physical mechanism at a time and reports its effect on threshold, subthreshold slope, output current and temperature behavior. Device width, finger geometry and layout parasitics must be treated explicitly when moving from a transistor model to a real amplifier.

sections.title: 7. From physical theory to circuit design
sections.html:
To design a common-source or differential-stage bias, first choose power/current and available supply swing. Obtain realistic transistor curves or PDK models; calculate \(g_m\), \(g_{ds}\), and capacitances around the actual operating point. Only then decide the gain, speed and noise budget. Use hand calculations to detect a mistaken bias, and simulator corner checks to explore process and temperature variability.

Do not present a hand-derived square-law current as a foundry simulation result. In reports, label analytical estimate, compact-model prediction, TCAD prediction and measurement separately.

example.title: From overdrive to gain efficiency and output resistance
example.problem: An illustrative long-channel NMOS has β = μn C′ox(W/L)=200 µA/V², VOV=0.20 V and an independent local channel-length-modulation parameter λ=0.08 V⁻¹. Estimate nominal saturated current and ideal gm from the square-law part, then a first-order ro at this current. State why the numbers are only approximate.
steps: The \(g_m\) and \(r_o\) estimates combine simple approximations; for a consistent finite-\(\lambda\) operating point, account for the chosen \(V_{DS}\) and extract both derivatives from the same local current model or simulated I–V data.

checks.prompt: Derive the triode-region I–V law by integrating a linearly decreasing inversion charge.
checks.hint: Write (|Q_i(x)|=C'_{ox}(V_{OV}-V)), then integrate (I_D dx=mu W|Q_i|dV) along the channel.

checks.prompt: For VGS=1.1 V and VT=0.45 V, what VDS marks the ideal long-channel saturation boundary?
checks.answer: \(V_{OV}=1.1-0.45=0.65\ \mathrm{V}\). Ideal long-channel saturation starts at about \(V_{DS}\ge0.65\ \mathrm{V}\), within model assumptions.

checks.prompt: With β=1 mA/V² and VOV=0.3 V, calculate ID,sat and gm.
A stage has gm=2 mS, ro=50 kΩ and RD=10 kΩ. Estimate gain ignoring other loads.
checks.hint: For AC-grounded supply and fixed source, (A_vapprox-g_m(R_Dparallel r_o)).

checks.prompt: Two NMOS devices have the same W/L, but one has a much shorter L. Must their measured ID–VG curves match?
checks.hint: What effects violate a simple long-channel W/L law?
checks.answer: No. Velocity saturation, DIBL, channel-length modulation, source/drain series resistance, mobility degradation and geometry-dependent threshold can alter current even at identical \(W/L\).

checks.prompt: If a circuit designer maximizes gm/ID without considering capacitance, does bandwidth automatically increase?
checks.answer: No. Bandwidth depends on \(g_m/C\), poles, parasitic loading and bias. A transistor can have favorable \(g_m/I_D\) while increased area and capacitance harm speed.

checks.prompt: For γ=0.4 V^0.5, 2φF=0.6 V, and VSB=0.4 V, estimate ΔVT.
checks.answer: \(\Delta V_T=0.4(\sqrt{1.0}-\sqrt{0.6})\approx0.4(1-0.77460)\approx0.0902\ \mathrm{V}\). This is a classical square-root estimate.
